reference.item: In backend/app/models.py, UserBase.email enforces a strict database-level unique constraint (Field(unique=True)). If a user is soft-deleted, their email remains in the table, meaning subsequent registration or signup attempts with that email will fail in crud.getuserbyemail or trigger an unhandled database IntegrityError.

In backend/app/api/routes/users.py, the admin deleteuser endpoint explicitly executes statement = delete(Item).where(col(Item.ownerid) == userid) before deleting the user. If an engineer converts user deletion to a soft delete but overlooks this query, the user's items will still be permanently deleted, directly violating the requirement to preserve them.

In backend/app/api/deps.py, getcurrentuser retrieves the user by primary key and only verifies if not user.isactive. If soft deletion is introduced with a new timestamp or boolean flag without deactivating the user or updating getcurrentuser, soft-deleted users with valid JWT tokens will remain authenticated until their tokens expire up to 8 days later.

In backend/app/api/routes/users.py, the readusers endpoint executes unfiltered queries for both the total count (select(func.count()).selectfrom(User)) and the retrieved batch (select(User)). Without adding filtering for soft-deleted records, deleted accounts will continue to appear in the admin user list and distort pagination counts.

Neither compose.yml nor the backend/ application defines any background task worker or scheduler (such as Celery, ARQ, or a cron runner). Without introducing infrastructure to periodically check and permanently purge accounts older than 30 days, expired accounts will remain in a soft-deleted state indefinitely.

In backend/app/api/routes/login.py, recoverpassword fetches users using crud.getuserbyemail without filtering by deletion status. This allows soft-deleted users to request recovery emails and potentially reset their passwords to regain active access without admin intervention.

There is currently no restore endpoint in the API or UI, and creating one without validation could allow admins to restore accounts beyond the 30-day cutoff or cause state conflicts if the email address was reused in the interim. It must also be defined whether restoring an account should reinstate isactive for users who were explicitly deactivated prior to deletion.

Existing unit and integration tests in backend/tests/api/routes/testusers.py (such as testdeleteuserme and testdeleteusersuperuser) explicitly query the database after deletion to assert that result is None. Modifying deletion behavior without updating these assertions and adding test coverage for item retention and the 30-day restore window will break the test suite in CI.

isactive flag overload – the UserBase model already defines isactive, which is used for account activation/login; repurposing it for soft‑delete may break existing authentication checks that treat a non‑active user as never‑registered.

In app/models.py, User.followingposts() explicitly includes the user's own posts via Author.id == self.id; reusing this query directly will erroneously include the recipient's own posts in their digest.

In app/email.py, sendemail() defaults to spawning a separate unmanaged background Thread for each email (sync=False); iterating over all users in a loop will launch hundreds or thousands of threads simultaneously, exhausting system memory and overwhelming the SMTP server.

The codebase lacks a recurring task scheduler, as the infrastructure in Procfile and deployment/supervisor/microblog-tasks.conf only runs a standard rq worker for on-demand user tasks; without introducing a scheduler like rq-scheduler or cron, there is no mechanism to trigger the digest weekly.

Generating absolute URLs for posts and profiles within email templates using urlfor(..., external=True) will fail or produce broken links in a background worker because SERVERNAME defaults to None in config.py and no HTTP request context is active.

In app/models.py, the User model contains no fields for email notification preferences or opt-out tokens; sending unsolicited digests without an unsubscribe mechanism violates CAN-SPAM/GDPR regulations and requires a database migration to track preferences.

Iterating through all users and querying their followed authors' recent posts will produce an O(N) database query bottleneck that will exhaust database connections and exceed the default execution timeout of the single configured RQ worker.

Filtering posts using a naive relative window like datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=7) without persisting a per-user lastdigestsent timestamp will cause posts to be duplicated or skipped whenever scheduled runs drift, fail, or are retried.

Timezone and date‑range mismatches – The Post.timestamp field is stored as UTC, but the digest must include only posts from the last week; failing to convert to the user’s local timezone could result in missing or duplicated entries.

Task progress tracking misuse – tasks.settaskprogress expects a Task entry per RQ job; the digest job would need its own Task record, otherwise the progress updates will raise AttributeError when task is None.

In styleguideexample/blogexamples/googleloginserverflow/sdk/apis.py and raw/apis.py, the callback reads idtokendecoded["email"] without checking the emailverified claim. If an attacker registers an unverified Google account using a target's email address, automatic linking will grant unauthorized access to an existing password-authenticated account.

When a user signs up via Google first, BaseUserManager.createuser assigns an unusable password via user.setunusablepassword(). Because UserCreateApi rejects existing emails and no password-setting or reset endpoints exist, that user will be permanently unable to set a password or authenticate through UserSessionLoginApi or UserJwtLoginApi.

While UserJwtLoginApi and UserSessionLoginApi return JWT tokens and session keys respectively, GoogleLoginApi only calls login(request, user) and returns raw Google tokens without returning a session key or generating a JWT. Clients relying on JSONWebTokenAuthentication or SessionAsHeaderAuthentication via ApiAuthMixin will be unable to authenticate subsequent API requests after Google sign-in.

GoogleLoginApi directly invokes Django's login(request, user) immediately upon finding a matching user, bypassing the isactive check that Django's authenticate() enforces during password logins. This allows inactive or deactivated accounts (isactive=False on BaseUser) to regain access simply by authenticating through Google.

BaseUserManager.createuser normalizes emails with self.normalizeemail(email.lower()), but GoogleLoginApi filters with userlist(filters={"email": useremail}), which performs a case-sensitive exact match. If Google returns an email with differing capitalization, the lookup will fail to link the account, triggering unexpected 404 errors or duplicate registration attempts.

Auto-provisioning missing accounts during Google login without atomic transactions or locking will race with concurrent password registrations (UserCreateApi) for the same email. This will crash the callback with an unhandled database IntegrityError due to the unique constraint on BaseUser.email.

BaseUser links identity exclusively via the mutable email string and contains no field or model to track Google's immutable subject identifier (sub). If a user changes their primary email address in either service, account linking breaks or risks associating a recycled email with an unintended user.

Google OAuth logic is currently split between two separate sample packages (blogexamples/googleloginserverflow/sdk and raw) rather than integrated into styleguideexample/authentication/. Implementing linking across or between these demonstration modules without consolidating into a single domain service creates divergent, hard-to-maintain authentication flows.

Adding post and patch to defaultRetryOptions.methods in source/utils/normalize.ts would cause Ky to retry on retry.statusCodes (such as 500, 502, 503, and 504) as well as network failures, violating the request to only retry when the network fails. This would re-execute failed server-side mutations for HTTP error responses that should have failed immediately.

Because POST and PATCH are non-idempotent methods, retrying on a NetworkError introduces duplicate server-side side effects if the connection was interrupted after the server received and processed the initial mutation. Ky has no way of discerning whether a network failure occurred before the request reached the server or after the server began handling it.

In source/core/Ky.ts, connection drops produce a NetworkError whereas request timeouts throw a TimeoutError, which is governed separately by retry.retryOnTimeout (defaulting to false). Flaky mobile connections frequently fail via timeouts, meaning the change would either fail to resolve mobile drops or, if retryOnTimeout is broadened, unsafely retry requests that the server is still actively executing.

In source/core/Ky.ts, #fetch() calls this.request.clone() whenever retry.limit > 0, which invokes ReadableStream#tee() on streaming bodies. Enabling retries for POST and PATCH by default will force every streaming upload to buffer unconsumed chunks in memory, risking excessive memory consumption or out-of-memory crashes on resource-constrained mobile devices.

If a POST or PATCH request body is a ReadableStream that was disturbed or locked during an interrupted initial attempt, Request.clone() in #fetch() will throw an unhandled TypeError on the retry attempt rather than recovering cleanly. This would cause flaky mobile requests to crash with native stream errors rather than surfacing a clean NetworkError.

When using onUploadProgress, streamRequest in source/utils/body.ts pipes the request body through a progress-tracking transform stream. Retrying an interrupted POST or PATCH upload will cause progress events to restart from 0%, triggering confusing progress regressions or duplicate completion events in client UIs.

Existing custom retry.shouldRetry hooks that return undefined rely on Ky falling through to default method checks that reject POST and PATCH. Enabling POST and PATCH retries by default would alter this fallback behavior, silently triggering retries for existing applications that expect undefined to reject non-idempotent requests.

This change directly breaks existing test assertions in test/retry.ts—specifically tests like 'not on POST' and 'NetworkError is not retried for non-retriable method (POST)'—which enforce that POST requests fail fast without retrying. Changing this default represents a breaking change in Ky's core HTTP semantics for existing consumers.

POST and PATCH mutations frequently carry headers such as Idempotency-Key or authorization nonces generated for a single attempt. Retrying automatically without re-running beforeRequest hooks or providing a mechanism to refresh request-specific tokens will cause backends to reject retried requests as duplicate or invalid submissions.

Compatibility with existing retry config – Projects may already specify a custom retry object that omits methods. Overriding the default could unintentionally extend the retry set, breaking assumptions in tests or CI pipelines.

Network‑error detection – Ky decides whether an error is “network” via isNetworkError. Certain mobile edge cases (e.g., DNS‑lookup failures) may be classified differently, causing inconsistent retry behavior for POST/PATCH versus GET.
Server‑side rate limiting – Automatic retries on POST/PATCH may repeatedly hit rate‑limit responses (429) and ignore afterStatusCodes handling, leading to rapid back‑off loops and possible bans.

In app/entrypoint.sh, migrations are preceded by python manage.py flush --no-input; mistakenly copying or adapting this development logic into app/entrypoint.prod.sh will wipe the production PostgreSQL database on every deployment.

Running python manage.py migrate automatically while the old web container is still serving traffic will crash the live application whenever a migration introduces backward-incompatible changes, such as renaming or dropping columns and tables.

Placing python manage.py migrate inside app/entrypoint.prod.sh will cause concurrent migration race conditions and table lock deadlocks if multiple replicas of the web container are launched simultaneously during rollout.

Migrations requiring ACCESS EXCLUSIVE table locks (such as adding non-null columns or altering constraints) will block concurrent read and write queries from the running web container, causing request timeouts on the live site.

In nginx/nginx.conf, the upstream is hardcoded to server web:8000;, which Nginx resolves via Docker DNS only at startup; starting a new side-by-side container under a different name or IP will not receive traffic without dynamic DNS re-resolution or an explicit Nginx reload.

Neither app/Dockerfile.prod nor docker-compose.prod.yml defines container health checks; without readiness checks, incoming traffic will be routed to the new container while migrations are still executing or before Gunicorn has finished binding to port 8000, triggering 502 Bad Gateway errors.

The web and nginx services share staticvolume at /home/app/web/staticfiles; running collectstatic for the new version while the old container is live will overwrite existing assets in place, causing cache mismatches and 404 errors for active user sessions.

Standard docker-compose commands do not natively support zero-downtime rolling replacements; attempting to start a new web container alongside the existing one will fail due to container name and network alias conflicts unless a blue-green orchestration strategy is introduced.

If an automatic database migration fails midway due to a constraint violation or invalid SQL, the deployment script may crash without an automated rollback strategy, leaving the database partially migrated and both container versions in a broken state.

When the old web container is terminated after the new one is up, in-flight operations—such as image uploads processed by upload/views.py—will be abruptly severed if Docker does not allow Gunicorn sufficient graceful shutdown time.
The script uses a simple nc loop with no timeout to wait for PostgreSQL; if the database never becomes reachable, the container will hang indefinitely, preventing new deployments from completing.

In src/app/routes/article/article.mapper.ts, articleMapper explicitly formats author: authorMapper(article.author, id). If this is replaced with an authors array rather than retaining the singular author field, existing Conduit API clients expecting a single author object will break.

In src/app/routes/article/article.service.ts, updateArticle generates newSlug as ${slugify(article.title)}-${id} using the authenticated user's ID. If a co-author edits the title, the slug will incorporate the co-author's ID instead of the original author's ID, mutating the slug and breaking existing article URLs.

In src/app/routes/article/article.service.ts, updateArticle and deleteArticle enforce permissions via existingArticle.author.id !== id. Without careful refactoring, this logic will either reject legitimate co-authors with a 403 Forbidden error on updates or naively allow any co-author to permanently delete an article without the primary author's consent.

In src/app/routes/article/article.service.ts, buildFindAllQuery filters by author using author: { AND: [{ username: { equals: query.author } }] }. If the underlying Prisma model transitions to multiple authors without updating this filter to inspect relation lists (e.g., authors: { some: ... }), querying GET /articles?author=:username will fail at runtime or omit co-authored articles.

In src/prisma/schema.prisma, Article currently defines a scalar authorId Int foreign key referencing User. Replacing authorId with a many-to-many relation without a careful migration script to backfill existing records into the new join table will corrupt foreign keys or cause permanent loss of existing authorship data.

In src/app/routes/article/article.service.ts, getFeed fetches articles matching author: { followedBy: { some: { id } } }. If this query is expanded to check multiple authors without applying distinct selection, users who follow more than one co-author of the same article will receive duplicate articles and corrupted pagination counts.

In src/app/routes/article/article.service.ts, favoriteArticle and unfavoriteArticle build response payloads directly using profileMapper(article.author, id) rather than articleMapper. Updating the Prisma include statements and response models only in articleMapper will cause runtime crashes during favorite/unfavorite operations due to referencing undefined article.author.

In src/app/routes/article/article.service.ts, createArticle only connects a single author via the authenticated user's ID. Introducing co-authors in the creation payload without validating user existence, preventing duplicate IDs, or establishing an authorization/invitation mechanism could allow arbitrary author impersonation or unhandled database constraint exceptions.
